details:
**"Ode on a Grecian Urn"**
Keats's most famous poem and the most common giveaway for him. The speaker addresses an ancient urn as a "still unravish'd bride of quietness," a "foster-child of silence and slow time," and a "Sylvan historian," and ends with the urn's message: "Beauty is truth, truth beauty, —that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know."

**Lines from the Grecian Urn**
Other often-quoted lines include "Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter"; "What leaf-fring'd legend haunts about thy shape?"; "What men or gods are these?"; "Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed / Your leaves"; and the question "To what green altar, O mysterious priest, / Lead'st thou that heifer lowing at the skies." The urn is also called an "Attic shape."

**"Ode to a Nightingale"**
The 1819 ode that begins "My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense" and ends "Fled is that music: —Do I wake or sleep?" just after asking "Was it a vision, or a waking dream?" The speaker calls the bird a "light-winged Dryad of the trees" and tells it "Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!"

**"Half in love with easeful Death"**
Lines from "Ode to a Nightingale" also used as clues: the speaker wants a "draught of vintage," a "beaker full of the warm South" with "beaded bubbles winking at the brim"; he flies "Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards, / But on the viewless wings of Poesy"; and he notes "tender is the night." The bird's song is the same one heard by Ruth when "she stood in tears amid the alien corn," and the word "forlorn" brings the speaker back to himself, admitting "the fancy cannot cheat so well / As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf."

**"La Belle Dame sans Merci"**
Keats's ballad, which opens "O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms, / Alone and palely loitering?" The knight, with "anguish moist and fever-dew," tells how he met a lady in the meads, a "faery's child," made her a garland, bracelets, and "fragrant zone," and was taken to her "elfin grot," then dreamed of "pale kings and princes too" warning that she had him "in thrall."

**"Adonais"**
Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1821 elegy for Keats, who died in Rome of tuberculosis at age 25. It opens "I weep for Adonais—he is dead!", asks where Urania was when he died, tells mourners to "Go thou to Rome," blames a hostile reviewer (a "nameless worm," a "noteless blot"), and ends with Keats's soul shining "like a star" from "the abode where the Eternal are."

**Endymion**
Keats's long four-book poem (1818) about the love of the moon goddess Cynthia for the shepherd prince Endymion. It begins "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever," and is dedicated to the memory of Thomas Chatterton. John Gibson Lockhart attacked it in Blackwood's Magazine, telling Keats, who had trained as an apothecary, that it is better to be a starved apothecary than a starved poet.

**"Ode to Psyche"**
The first of the 1819 odes, addressed to the goddess Psyche, who was deified too late to have been worshipped in antiquity. The speaker offers to "be thy choir, and make a moan / Upon the midnight hours" and says "Yes, I will be thy priest, and build a fane / In some untrodden region of my mind," and the poem ends by leaving a window open "To let the warm Love in."

**"Ode on Melancholy" and "Ode on Indolence"**
Two more of the 1819 odes. "Ode on Melancholy" advises the reader to "glut thy sorrow on a morning rose" and, "if thy mistress some rich anger shows, / Emprison her soft hand, and let her rave," and says that "in the very temple of Delight / Veil'd Melancholy has her sovran shrine." In "Ode on Indolence," three figures in "placid sandals, and in white robes" (Love, Ambition, and Poesy) pass by, and the final stanza begins "So, ye three Ghosts, adieu!"

**"To Autumn"**
Keats's 1819 ode to the "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, / Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun." It pictures Autumn on a "granary floor" and by a "cider-press," asks "Where are the songs of spring?", and ends with "hedge-crickets" singing and "gathering swallows" twittering in the skies. In a letter to John Hamilton Reynolds, Keats said he had never liked stubble fields so much as on the walk that inspired it.

**"On First Looking into Chapman's Homer"**
Keats's 1816 sonnet about reading George Chapman's translation of Homer. It begins "Much have I travell'd in the realms of gold" and compares the experience to "some watcher of the skies / When a new planet swims into his ken" and to "stout Cortez" staring at the Pacific, "silent, upon a peak in Darien" (the explorer who actually saw it first was Balboa).

**"When I have fears that I may cease to be"**
A sonnet in which Keats fears dying before his pen has "glean'd my teeming brain." He imagines "huge cloudy symbols of a high romance" that he may never "trace / Their shadows, with the magic hand of chance," and ends standing alone "on the shore / Of the wide world" until "love and fame to nothingness do sink."

**"Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art"**
A sonnet associated with Keats's fiancée Fanny Brawne, in which the speaker wishes to lie on his love's breast, "Awake for ever in a sweet unrest." It gave its name to Jane Campion's 2009 film Bright Star about their romance.

**Hyperion**
Keats's unfinished epic about the overthrow of the Titans by the Olympians, in which the fallen Saturn appears and Hyperion asks whether he too will fall. It breaks off with the word "Celestial" as Apollo, gazing into the eyes of Mnemosyne, is transformed into a god. Keats later recast it as The Fall of Hyperion.

**Keats's letters: "negative capability" and the "vale of Soul-making"**
In an 1817 letter to his brothers, Keats defined "negative capability," the ability to remain in "uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts" without reaching after fact and reason, a quality he said Shakespeare possessed. Other letters compare life to a "Mansion of Many Apartments" and describe the world as "a vale of Soul-making," with the heart as "the Mind's Bible." Late fragments include "This living hand," which would "haunt thy days and chill thy dreaming nights," and the sonnet "On Sitting Down to Read King Lear Once Again," which asks for "new Phoenix wings."
